## Previously ...

Six lectures analysing Loomrow's data, ending in a published dashboard. Every
number in it came from a file somebody else handed you.

. . .

Two questions a supplied dataset never forces:

- What was worth recording in the first place?
- What can this number actually prove?

. . .

**Today we build the thing we are going to measure, so that both questions
become yours.**

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Build and publish a small multi-page site suitable for tracking
- Identify the user actions on that site that carry commercial meaning
- Write a statement of success **before** any tracking exists

# 1. Why Build Before Measuring

## The Problem With Borrowed Data

<!-- Speaker notes: the standard analytics module hands students a clean sample
     dataset. Students learn the tool but never learn the judgement, because
     they never had to decide what was worth recording. Loomrow was deliberately
     that module for six weeks; this is the pivot. -->

`insta-data.csv` was clean, complete and rectangular. Somebody decided that
`reach_followers` and `reach_non_followers` were worth splitting out, and you
inherited that decision without ever making it.

. . .

That is the shape of most analytics teaching, and of a lot of analytics work. It
produces people who are fluent in tools and helpless about measurement.

. . .

**From today the decisions are yours, and so are the consequences.**

## The Portfolio as a Business

Your site is not a CV. It is a **business with an objective**, and it is the
object of study for the rest of the module.

. . .

That means it needs something a visitor can *do*:

- Send an enquiry
- Sign up to something
- Download something
- Book a slot

. . .

**A site nobody can act on generates page views and nothing else**, and page
views cannot carry the second half of this module.

# 2. Site Structure

## Minimum Viable Structure

Four pages. No more, for now.

- **Home**: who you are and what you offer, above the fold
- **Work**: two or three case studies, each its own page or anchor
- **About**: the human bit
- **Contact**: the page that exists to be a conversion

. . .

The fourth page is the one that matters. **One page must exist purely to be
converted on**, whether that is a form, a download or a booking link.

## Tooling Options {.smaller}

| Option | Cost | Control | Tagging |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quarto + GitHub Pages** | Free | Total | Trivial: one line in `_quarto.yml` |
| **Plain HTML + GitHub Pages** | Free | Total | Trivial, but you write everything |
| **Wix, Squarespace, Carrd** | Paid tiers | Limited | Possible, often behind a plan |
| **Notion, Canva sites** | Free tiers | Very limited | Frequently impossible |

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**The hard constraint: you must be able to inject a script into `<head>` on every
page.** Check this before you build anything. A platform that will not let you is
a platform you cannot use for this module.
:::

. . .

**The default for this module is Quarto published to GitHub Pages**, because it
is free, versioned, and the tag goes in one file.

## Why GitHub, Beyond Hosting

GitHub is a code-collaboration platform that quietly became several other
things. Two matter here:

- **File and code storage with version control.** Every change to your site is
  recorded, dated and reversible
- **Online publication.** GitHub Pages hosts a static site straight out of a
  repository, free, over HTTPS

. . .

You will use the same account again in Lecture 13 for notebooks, and in
Assignment 2.

## Creating the Repository {.smaller}

1. Top right, the `+` menu → **New repository**
2. **A short, memorable name.** No spaces; `snake_case` or `kebab-case`
3. Optionally a description
4. **Public**. Pages does not serve a private repository on the free tier
5. Tick **Add a README file**
6. **Create repository**

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Name it carefully. The repository name becomes part of your public URL, and
renaming it later breaks every link you have shared, including the ones in your
GA4 property.
:::

## Turning On GitHub Pages

1. **Settings** → **Pages** in the left pane
2. Under **Branch**, change `None` to `main`, and **Save**
3. **Actions**, and wait for *pages build and deployment* to finish

. . .

Your site is then at:

```
https://<username>.github.io/<repository>/
```

. . .

So for the user `damien-dupre` and the repository `portfolio`, that is
`https://damien-dupre.github.io/portfolio/`. **Write your URL down. Lecture 9
needs it.**

## The Quarto Site {.smaller}

A Quarto website is a folder of `.qmd` files plus one configuration file:

```{.yaml}
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Your Name"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: work.qmd
        text: Work
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
      - href: contact.qmd
        text: Contact
```

. . .

`quarto render` turns it into a `_site/` folder of plain HTML. **That folder is
what GitHub Pages serves.**

## The One Line That Matters

Also in `_quarto.yml`, and the reason this toolchain was chosen:

```{.yaml}
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    include-in-header: head.html
```

. . .

Whatever is in `head.html` is injected into `<head>` on **every page of the
site, from one file**. Next week that file holds your Google tag.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A tag that fires on the homepage but not on the contact page is the single most
common cause of a broken funnel. This pattern is how you avoid it.
:::

## Live Demo {background="#43464B"}

<!-- Speaker notes: fifteen minutes, and it always runs long. Have a repository

1. Create the repository, public, with a README

3. `quarto render`, and look at `_site/`

# 3. Defining Success Before Tracking

## The Pre-Registration Habit

Experimental science has a rule: **write down what you expect to find before you
look.** Otherwise every result is a finding, because the hypothesis moves.

. . .

Marketing analytics has no such norm, and suffers for it. A month of traffic can
be made to look like a success by anyone allowed to choose the metric
afterwards.

. . .

**So choose it now, while you still have no data and nothing to defend.**

## The Success Statement {.smaller}

One paragraph, written today, kept for the rest of the module:

> *This site is for **[audience]**. Success is **[a specific action]**. A good
> month is **[a number]** of them. I will conclude it is not working if
> **[a condition]**.*

. . .

Worked example:

> *This site is for Dublin agency recruiters hiring junior analysts. Success is a
> completed contact form. A good month is five. I will conclude it is not working
> if fewer than 100 people reach the work page in a month, because then the
> problem is traffic, not the site.*

. . .

Note what the last clause buys you: a **failure condition that distinguishes two
different problems**. That is what makes it worth writing.

## Objectives Are Not Metrics

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

**Not an objective**

- "Build my brand"
- "Increase engagement"
- "Get noticed"

None of these names an action, so none of them can be recorded, so none of them
can be wrong.

:::

::: {#second-column}

**An objective**

- "Five completed contact forms a month"
- "Half of work-page visitors reach the bottom"

Each names an action, a count and a period.

:::
::::

. . .

This distinction is the whole of Lecture 9, brought forward by a week.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

Write the success statement for your own site. Four sentences, in your notes,
where you will still have them in April:

1. Who is the site for?
2. What single action counts as success?
3. How many of those make a good month?
4. What would make you conclude it is not working?

Then say it out loud to the person beside you. **If they can argue the number,
it is specific enough.**

::: {#timer1 .timer seconds="900"}
:::

# 4. Vibe Coding Your Site

## AI This Block: Chat

Where we are on the module's AI spine, set out in Lecture 1 and named properly in
Lecture 12:

> **Chat.** A tutor. Ask it to explain, and to type. Not to decide.

## Building a Site by Describing It

An assistant will produce a working Quarto site from a description faster than
you can write one, and this is a good use of it: the site is scaffolding, not the
thing being assessed.

. . .

> "Create a four-page Quarto website: home, work, about, contact. The contact
> page has a form. Give me `_quarto.yml` and one page as an example, and show me
> where a script tag would go in `<head>` for every page."

. . .

Then read every line before you publish it. **You are publishing this under your
own name, at a URL you will put on a CV.**

## What You Must Still Decide Yourself

- **What the site is for.** No assistant can tell you, and it will invent
  something plausible if you let it
- **Which action counts as a conversion.** A commercial judgement about your own
  work
- **Whether the generated page actually loads the tag** on every page, which you
  verify by looking, not by asking

. . .

**Delegate the typing. Keep the deciding.** Students who let an assistant design
their measurement cannot analyse their own data in April, and it shows.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Generate a site skeleton by describing it to an assistant
2. Read the output and list two things you would change
3. Publish it to GitHub Pages and open the live URL
4. View source on **two different pages** and confirm you can see where a script
   in `<head>` would land

Step 4 is the one Lecture 9 depends on. Do not leave without it.
